I guess the best place to start is the beginning. Before the inflation started the universe was still infinitely big (from our perspective), it was just infinitely dense. Think about it this way: the universe was way more dense than all of the known black holes so even if we wanted to leave we'd never find the edge. Functionally the universe was infinitely large before the "big bang".

Then the inflation started. What does it mean for something that's infinitely large to inflate? It means that it becomes less dense and a larger infinity. Since it's something without edges growing that means that it grows from all points at once. New space was being created at all points, and it was happening very very fast. So we have functionally infinite energy density expanding. What this means is that it cooled off fast. As the cooling happened the energy dropped enough for actual matter to precipitate from the energy. It was protons that precipitated first. Since there was matter (hydrogen ions) and lots of energy (heat) nuclear fusion started occurring almost immediately. The hydrogen ions were able to fuse into Helium and Lithium before it cooled down. All of this happened in the space of the first five minutes of the universe. The expansion continued, and the universe continued to cool for the next ~300,000 years.

After cooling and expanding for 300,000 years the universe became "thin" enough for light to travel. This is as far back into the universe as we can see (the further away something is in space, the further back in time it is). This is the edge of the visible universe. As the universe expanded pockets of matter attracted other matter. These pockets would get dense enough that nuclear fusion started. This was the first generation of stars and galaxies. These stars were crucibles that created all of the elements up to Iron on the periodic table from the building blocks of hydrogen, helium and lithium. As these stars died some of them went supernova which created all of the elements heavier than iron.

This cycle of star formation and star death continued as the universe expanded, but since the medium is getting thinner each generation has had less stars. This is going to continue until star formation effectively stops. The only things that will be left in the universe are white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. The white dwarfs will cool into brown dwarfs, the neutron stars will go dark, and finally the last of the black holes will evaporate and the universe will be a thin shell of what it was full of nothing but ash.

I see the heat death of the universe as the ultimate Sisyphean challenge of civilization, a seemingly impossible to overcome, always looming for as long as time shall endure. I, like many, hope it will eventually be overcome via as of yet to be discovered physics, but the current prospects are not promising. I'm not however personally concerned about the struggle whatsoever. My concern is my cosmically ephemeral lifespan. If immediately impending death were conquered within my lifetime, for a great many millennia I wouldn't be concerned with the problem. If after all that time I am still alive and interested in living indefinitely, I would be disappointed if a solution hadn't yet presented itself. At that point if there are still seemingly discoverable known unknowns, then I would start investing a serious percentage of my time and effort into trying to solve the problem by spoiling the rest of the remaining known unknowns. I wouldn't however torture myself over the problem. I was born with death looming and if I can ever overcome immediate death, I'll consider myself fortunate to have overcome that grim fate, and I will learn to accept my return to an eventual inevitable death.
